question: Tell me about a time you sought candid feedback on your own work and it stung. What did you do with it?

raiseTranscript.text: I asked my mentor to review a feature spec I wrote in my first month. She said the success metrics were vague and the user flow assumptions were off. It stung because I had spent a week on it.
I rewrote the metrics section with actual numbers from our logs and scheduled a 30-minute follow-up. I also added two edge cases she flagged. The second version got used in planning.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you sought candid feedback on your own work and it stung. What did you do with it?
Role: new engineer on first feature spec
Action: rewrote metrics with log data and added edge cases after one round of feedback
Outcome: spec used in planning meeting
Quote: 'It stung because I had spent a week on it.'
Follow-up: Asked how they handled the emotional part; said they waited 24 hours then focused on concrete changes
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar. The candidate proactively asked for feedback on their own work and translated stinging input into a revised spec that was actually adopted. Story shows quick iteration on concrete items rather than defensiveness. At junior level this demonstrates the coachability we need. Biggest strength is turning feedback into a usable artifact within one cycle.

lowerTranscript.text: My manager told me my code review comments were too nitpicky. It hurt because I was trying to be thorough.
I tried to be nicer but didn't really change how I reviewed. I figured it was just their preference.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you sought candid feedback on your own work and it stung. What did you do with it?
Action: said they 'tried to be nicer' but kept same approach
Outcome: no visible change in behavior or results
Quote: 'I figured it was just their preference.'
Follow-up: Asked for example of a changed review; none provided
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar. Candidate reports receiving direct feedback but shows no evidence of adjusting their approach or measuring impact. At junior level we expect visible iteration on personal work; here the response stays at the level of feeling without action. Biggest gap is lack of follow-through on the feedback received.

raiseTranscript.text: I ran a retro on a cross-team launch I led and asked the other team’s tech lead for blunt input on my coordination. He said I had under-communicated trade-off decisions, which created last-minute work for them.
I wrote up the specific decisions I had skipped sharing, sent it to both teams, and started a weekly sync note. Their next launch had fewer escalations.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you sought candid feedback on your own work and it stung. What did you do with it?
Action: documented skipped trade-offs and added weekly sync note
Outcome: fewer escalations on next launch
Quote: 'He said I had under-communicated trade-off decisions.'
Follow-up: Asked how they got the other team to adopt the new process; said they proposed it in the retro and followed up in writing
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar. Candidate sought feedback from a peer on cross-team coordination and converted it into a repeatable process that reduced escalations. Shows influence without authority and measurable team-level impact. At senior level this is the expected pattern. Biggest strength is turning personal feedback into a coordination improvement that benefited another team.

lowerTranscript.text: A peer told me my project updates were too high-level for their team. I felt it was unfair since I was already sending weekly notes.
I added a one-sentence summary but kept the same format. They still complained sometimes.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you sought candid feedback on your own work and it stung. What did you do with it?
Action: added one sentence but kept format unchanged
Quote: 'I felt it was unfair since I was already sending weekly notes.'
Follow-up: Asked for before/after example of a note; candidate could not produce one
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar. Feedback was received but the candidate made only a token adjustment and did not test whether it addressed the root issue. At senior level we look for cross-team leverage and clear before/after results; neither appears here. Biggest gap is minimal adaptation with no evidence of impact.

raiseTranscript.text: After our re-org I asked two directors who now reported to me for direct feedback on my leadership style. One said I was still operating at the VP level and not delegating enough strategic context.
I stopped attending their staff meetings, created a monthly strategy memo instead, and tracked how many decisions they made without me. Two quarters later their teams owned roadmap trade-offs.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you sought candid feedback on your own work and it stung. What did you do with it?
Action: stopped attending staff meetings, shifted to monthly memo, measured decisions owned by directs
Outcome: directs' teams owned roadmap trade-offs within two quarters
Quote: 'I was still operating at the VP level and not delegating enough strategic context.'
Follow-up: Asked how they handled the emotional reaction at their level; said they took a week to process then focused on org leverage
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar. Candidate solicited feedback from new directs on their own leadership and made structural changes that increased delegation at the org level. Demonstrates long-term thinking and leverage through others. At exec level this is the standard. Biggest strength is converting personal feedback into measurable ownership shift for two teams.

lowerTranscript.text: A peer exec told me my skip-levels were too tactical. It was uncomfortable.
I mentioned it in my next staff meeting and asked my directs to handle more. I didn't track whether it stuck.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you sought candid feedback on your own work and it stung. What did you do with it?
Action: mentioned in staff meeting but no follow-up mechanism
Outcome: no tracking or reported change
Follow-up: Asked for org-level metric that improved; none given
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar. Feedback was acknowledged but the candidate stopped at a single mention without creating accountability or measuring org impact. At exec level we expect strategic delegation and visible leverage; the story shows neither. Biggest gap is absence of sustained action or results tied to the feedback.
